===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*terh₁-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|throwen}}, {{m|enm|thrawen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|þrāwan|t=to turn, twist}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*þrāan}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*þrēaną|t=to twist, turn}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*terh₁-|t=to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn}}.

Cognate with {{cog|sco|thraw|t=to twist, turn, throw}}, {{cog|fy|triuwe|t=to push}}, {{cog|nl|draaien|t=to turn}}, {{cog|nds|draien}}, {{m|nds|dreien|t=to turn (in a lathe)}}, {{cog|de|drehen|t=to turn}}.

{{displaced|en|sl=1|warp}} as the word for hurling and was {{displaced|en|nocap=1|sl=1|by=1|warp}} as the word for twisting.

The use in computing comes from the fact, that in programming languages a statement reporting an error interrupts normal processing and sends an error object up the function calling stack until a handling statement intercepts it. Thus an “object” is “thrown” and “flies” until it is “caught”.

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:hore}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*keh₂-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|hore}}, from {{inh|en|ang|hōre}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*hōrǭ}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*kéh₂ros|t=loved}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*keh₂-|t=to wish; desire}}. Cognate with {{cog|nl|hoer}}, {{cog|de|Hure}}, {{cog|non|hóra}} as well as {{cog|sa|चारु|tr=cā́ru||dear}}, {{cog|la|cārus||dear, expensive}}, and {{cog|ga|cara||friend}}. 

The unetymological spelling with ''wh-'' superficially denotes a formerly standard pronunciation with an excrescent {{IPAchar|/w/}} (such as in {{m|en|whole}}), but such a form is hardly found in either commentators on Early Modern English pronunciations or records of traditional dialects (which both explicitly mention its rarity or absence), therefore leaving the spelling somewhat inexplicable.<ref name="Dobson">{{R:en:Dobson:1957|II|430|998}}</ref> However, this may be because such an excrescent {{IPAchar|/w/}} was absorbed by a following {{IPAchar|/uː/}} (as in words with etymological {{IPAchar|/w/}} such as {{m|en|whom}}, {{m|en|two}}) after it became established in the spelling but before our earliest orthoepic records.

===Verb===

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[prove]] (something) to be [[false]] or [[incorrect]].
#: {{syn|en|debunk|disprove|rebut|confound}}
#: {{ant|en|confirm|affirm|demonstrate|prove}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|proscribed}} To [[deny]] the [[truth]] or [[correctness]] of (something); to reject or disagree with an accusation.
#: {{syn|en|dispute|deny|repudiate|rebut|gainsay|counterargue|reject}}
#: {{ant|en|affirm|accept|embrace|profess}}
#* {{RQ:Guardian|author=Taro Kaneko|title=Family ‘banned from more than 1,000 petrol stations’ amid fuel theft row|passage=A spokesperson for VARS Technology said: “We completely refute the suggestion that our market-leading ANPR system is unreliable".|date=20 December 2025|url=https://www.theguardian.com/money/2025/dec/20/fuel-theft-row-banned-petrol-stations-cash}}

====Usage notes====
* The second meaning of {{m|en|refute||to deny the truth of}} is [[proscribed]] as [[erroneous]] by some [http://books.google.co.uk/books?id=2yJusP0vrdgC&pg=PA807&lpg=PA807&dq=english+usage+refute&source=web&ots=nYrYodyZZ4&sig=G_alFFyWi7ZFBMYnaujrrrh9qUM&hl=en&sa=X&oi=book_result&resnum=4&ct=result| (compare Merriam Webster,1994)]. An alternative term with such a meaning is {{m|en|repudiate}}, which means to reject or refuse to acknowledge, but without the implication of justification.
* ''Refute'' is also often confused with ''[[rebut]]''; a ''[[rebuttal]]'', in formal debate terms, is a counter-refutation, and it also has a specific legal sense, though like ''[[refutation]]'', the word has taken on the informal and disputed meaning of ''[[denial]]''.

# {{senseid|en|Q5880}} {{lb|en|anatomy}} A [[sex organ]] for [[copulation]] and [[birth]], found in [[female]] [[therian]] [[mammal]]s, consisting of a passage between the [[vulval vestibule]] and the [[cervix]] of the [[uterus]].
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:vagina}}
#: {{hyper|en|internal genitalia|;|Müllerian duct|paramesonephric duct|urogenital sinus}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1991|author=Richard Evan Jones|title=Human Reproductive Biology|page=61|isbn=9780123897701
|text=The epithelial lining of the '''vagina''' consists of many layers of flattened cells. Changes in the condition of these cells during the menstrual cycle can be detected by swabbing the lining and looking at the cells under a microscope.}}
## {{lb|en|zootomy}} A similar organ in some [[invertebrate]]s and non-mammalian [[amniote]]s.
# {{lb|en|botany}} A [[sheathlike]] structure, such as the [[leaf]] of a [[grass]] that [[surround]]s a [[stem]].
#: {{syn|en|sheath}}
# {{lb|en|colloquial}} The [[vulva]], or the vulva and vaginal passage collectively.
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:vulva}}
#* {{see citations|en}}
# {{lb|en|derogatory|colloquial|rare}} A [[coward]]; a [[weakling]]; a [[pussy]].
#* '''2002''', "{{w|The New Terrance And Phillip Movie Trailer}}" (''South Park'' TV episode)
#*: {{quote|en|Don't you interrupt me, you '''vagina'''! I was givin' a heart-wrenchin' soliloquy about me feelin's for Tugger!}}
# {{lb|en|transgender slang|and|gay slang|uncommon}} The [[anus]].

====Usage notes====
* In technical discussions of anatomy, the {{m|en||vagina}} is a wholly internal structure and the {{m|en||vulva}} is wholly external, but in common use (since at least the 1930s)<ref>Besides [[Citations:vagina|these examples from the 1930s onward]], Martha Kirkpatrick, in ''Women’s Sexual Development: Explorations of Inner Space'' (2012), notes that a psychiatrist character played by a real psychiatrist uses ''vagina'' to include the vulva in the 1969 film ''Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice'', and cites another such use from 1970.</ref> the term {{m|en||vagina}} can refer to the {{m|en||vulva}}, or to the vulva and vaginal passage collectively.

====Usage notes====
The object of "avenge" is generally the act of injury or the injured party, never (in modern usage) the injuring party. The injuring party may be specified with "on," as in "to avenge X on his killer," but this is rather more common with "take/get revenge" and "[[revenge]] oneself" than with "avenge."

Compare {{m|en|bulldagger}}, attested since around the same time and used especially by black women.JoAnne Myers, ''Historical Dictionary of the Lesbian and Gay Liberation Movements'' (2013), p. 97Yetta Howard, ''Ugly Differences: Queer Female Sexuality in the Underground'' (2018), p. 238, which also refers to "Bogus, “The 'Queen B,'” and Walker, “The Debutante in Harlem,” 58–102, and “Lesbian Pulp in Black and White,” 103–138, for considerations of the figure of the black bulldagger in other Harlem Renaissance texts." Other linguists suggested that ''bull dyke(r)'' referred to strong black women who dug dikes, or derived from {{m|en|bull}} + {{m|en|dick}}, perhaps in reference to black men.Charles Panati, ''Sexy Origins and Intimate Things'' (1998), p. 181: "In fact, “bulldiking” is one of the earliest phrases in which the term “dike" has tough female overtones. It appeared in the American South in the nineteenth century, used by black Americans. Some linguists believe that strong black women who helped dig watercourses on Southern plantations were called “bulldikes.” Others, however, claim that "dike" is really a corruption of "dick", slang for "penis," and [...] argue that in the American South, black men who worked on plantations were called "bull dicks" by their white owners." It has also been suggested ''dyke'' is a shortening of {{m|en|morphodyke}}, from ''[[morphodite]]'', from ''[[hermaphrodite]]'',{{cite-book|en|year=1991|author=Sterling K. Eisiminger|title=The Consequence of Error and Other Language Essays|publisher=Peter Lang Pub Incorporated|text=Archibald Hill suggests that both dike and dyke are respectively clipped forms of morphodite and morphodyke, themselves clipped and mispronounced forms of hermaphrodite (A.S. 57.1).}} but the derivation may go in the other direction instead, with ''morphodyke'' being a blend of ''morphodite'' with the already-extant word ''dyke''. ====Noun==== {{en-noun}} {{tlb|en|slang|vulgar|usually|derogatory|and|offensive}} # {{sid|en|lesbian}} {{lb|en|anti-LGBTQ slur}} A [[lesbian]], particularly one with [[masculine]] or [[butch]] [[trait]]s or [[behavior]];
